title: Refactor the BlenderBIM Add-on to perform incremental editing
body:
**No new IFC export functionality is planned until this task is complete. Also, no new release will be made until this is fixed.**

This is a tracking issue for the general goal to migrate the BlenderBIM Add-on code to become an incremental editor. It'll take a while until this is closed.

In short, the BlenderBIM Add-on currently functions primarily as an importer and exporter. In other words, it parses the entire IFC dataset atomically, then imports it into Blender. During export, it does the inverse, it parses the entire Blender scene atomically, then exports it into IFC. This creates problems:

 1. Lots of data loss. The Blender data model will never fully match the IFC data model. We do a damn good job already (i.e. visibly better to a user compared to proprietary authoring apps), but we're still missing 30% of the spec.
 2. Long, very inefficient import / export times. So long as this is the case, it becomes a pain to use IFC as a source of truth. If this issue is not solved, it also impacts drawing generation efficiency (see #1153). Drawings are IFC based, and if we cannot very rapidly and continuously export and access the latest IFC data, that slows down our ability to then generate a drawing from it. It also impacts parametric geometry support (half solved, now). Drawings is one example, but the same applies for clash detection, COBie, and everything else.
 3. Lack of code modularity. This creates an unscalable maintenance nightmare, as the entire BIM model is treated atomically.
 4. Very difficult to scale to collaborative editing paradigms - with this new approach, users can only partially load what's interesting, Blender can more easily handle huuuuuuge models, and theoretically work across many apps, and changes even versioned logically without expensive reverse engineered diffs ... this new approach will make it possible in the future to implement multi user editing, not just within Blender, but across other applications too.
 5. Lots of operations cannot be made headless or authoring application agnostic - more and more experience with IfcPatch, IfcSverchok, and seeing what's happening in FreeCAD demonstrate that there is a huge amount of double-up. With an incremental editor, editing is done via ... well, IFC editing! Not translation, so the code can be reused across FreeCAD, NewCloudBIMApp, and so on.
 6. Difficult to write test cases for, as import / export is atomic and depends on Blender. If you can't test it, you can't trust it.
 7. Difficult to onboard new potential developers. Due to the atomic nature of the import / export process, developers will never be able to be sure of the scope and dependency flow of their changes. I've already tried my best to decouple the export code as much as possible, and those familiar with the existing code will realise that I've already decoupled parsing the Blender scene from the actual IFC authoring, so although it looks monolithic and scary, it should be able to be broken down quite easily and also make it easier for future devs.
 8. Errors are only discovered at export time. This can lead to a very slow, ambiguous, and annoying cleanup process, and requires the user to have previous knowledge of what the exporter expects.
 9. It discourages using dedicated UX/UI for BIM aspects that don't translate well to a Blender interface. For example, spreadsheeting, mass data manipulation, resolving change conflicts, paperspace... this new approach will allow many dedicated tools to augment Blender's capabilities, rather than trying to force everything into the Blender paradigm. This will allow other applications to do what they do best, and Blender to do what it does best, and they can both work together.

For the BlenderBIM Add-on to become the best IFC authoring application, it has to only not only operate using the IFC data model, it has to do it live, decoupled from the full Blender scene. This is what is meant by "incremental editing", or partial editing. In short, the IFC dataset, whether it is atomic or a subset of a greater central repository, shall be held in memory (in a file scenario), or if not, accessible via a standardised API. The import process therefore does not need to theoretically translate the entire model into the Blender environment. It can only partially import / visualise / display what's needed. Then, actions in Blender will edit the IFC dataset on the fly. The export process then does no IFC processing whatsoever, and just turns into a disk write operation (in a file scenario - in a central database scenario, there are options too, but let's keep this simple for now). This means faster imports, ultra-fast exports, no data loss, and the Blender editing functions naturally then segment themselves into modules - a module which only edits geometry, a module which only edits materials, a module which only edits documents, and so on.

There are disadvantages to this approach:

 1. It's a lot of work, and a lot of rework. Basically all the current functionality needs to be rebuilt. (Well, theoretically, mostly refactored, but still a lot of work)
 2. Some UI aspects in Blender may need rethinking. E.g. the simple action of duplicating an object now may create complications. Another example is when the user presses undo. The UX needs to make it clear that Blender is _not_ the BIM model ... Blender is simply a client through which it can view and modify portions of the BIM model.

The good news is that the initial attempts to move into this direction are already positive. The new [full native roundtripping feature](https://community.osarch.org/discussion/215/full-native-representation-roundtripping-in-the-blenderbim-add-on) effectively uses this approach already very successfully. With that option enabled, there is zero geometry data loss. Cool, right? What if that was everything? Also, after commit c844076 with that option enabled, you can edit parametric geometry, and export blazing fast.

**Modules which are basically done** (can always be improved, but enough that it works)

 - Aggregates (medium)
 - Attributes (medium)
 - BCF (easy)
 - BIMTester (easy) (thanks @ihabelaghoury !)
 - Clash (easy)
 - Classification (hard)
 - COBie (easy) (thanks @ihabelaghoury !)
 - Contexts (medium)
 - Constraint (medium)
 - Covetool (easy)
 - CSV (easy) (thanks @ihabelaghoury !)
 - Debug (easy)
 - Diff (easy) (thanks @ihabelaghoury !)
 - Document (medium)
 - Drawing (easy, apparently? Note: does not address #1153 at all - only prevents regressions)
 - Geometry (very hard)
 - Georeferencing (medium)
 - IfcSverchok (easy)
 - Material (hard)
 - Model (medium) (known regression for drawing support - will reimplement in future release)
 - Owner History (medium)
 - Patch (easy)
 - Presentation Layers (medium)
 - Project (medium)
 - Pset (hard)
 - PSet Template Definitions (easy)
 - Qto utilities (easy)
 - Root (medium)
 - Search (easy)
 - Spatial (easy)
 - Style (medium)
 - Type (easy)
 - Unit (easy)
 - Void (medium)

**Modules / functionality that we will delay implementation until a future release**

- BIM Server Library (medium) (minimal existing implementation, likely never used by a single user)
- Group (medium) (minimal existing implementation, so user won't miss anything)
- Structural (very hard) (minimal existing implementation, so user won't miss anything) (ping @ihabelaghoury )

Watch this space.

title: Is there code that handles removing an element including its dependencies?
body:
Let's say I have an IfcWall, or IfcShapeRepresentation, or IfcRepresentationItem, or anything that I might want to remove. I can do `ifc_file.remove(element)`, but that only removes the element itself, and doesn't recurse down to its dependencies. For example, I'd also want to remove the object placement, or representations of that IfcWall. However, I'd want to remover it intelligently, so that if the representation is mapped, the other mapped items remain unaffected. Or if there is a cartesian point used elsewhere, that won't get removed.

To solve this, I expect I'd need to build a graph and do a bit of voodoo. Is there already code out there that helps in this or maybe has solved it already, maybe something in C++?

I'm also curious is there can ever be a generic solution to this? E.g. for deleting a wall, it needs to consider what it does to opening elements and the products that fill those openings... are those products that fill the openings deleted too, or do they simply lose the fill relationship and become contained of the spatial element that the wall was contained in? Does this need to be considered case by case? Given that example, I would say ... yes?

Also, ideally performance should be reasonable - I've come across issues doing removes especially on large files.

body:
I've been using BIMTester integrated with IfcOpenShell to validate an IFC file for IFC Rail, and I've come across a problem.

It seems that IfcOpenShell does not recognize the serialization of [SELECT ](https://standards.buildingsmart.org/IFC/DEV/IFC4_3/RC2/HTML/link/ifcfacilityparttypeselect.htm)for IfcFacilityPart. In particular,  STEP serializes the SELECT for the PredefinedType by wrapping the value with the class name. 

I tried modifying the IFC file by writing the predefined type argument as an Enum (as it was in IFC 4.2) and passes the validation.
Is it possible to fix this?

Here an **Example**:

*this is how the STEP file should be written in 4.3*
=IFCFACILITYPART(‘2rZAYplcf7Hu4GBw_FfuTH’,$,'CircularQuay’,$,$,$,$,$,$,**IFCMARINEPARTTYPEENUM(.BERTHINGSTRUCTURE.),**.NOTDEFINED.);

*this is how it was done in 4.2 and it is recognized by IfcOpenShell*

Below are all the scenarios I can think of. A few things which I'm confused by:

 3. I guess scenario C has a similar priority but for non 2D shapes?

In the past, I generally disabled INCLUDE_CURVES by default because I noticed some elements that had 3D bodies would be processed as 2D curves instead. But this was a long time ago and maybe I wasn't using the iterator, or maybe there is something I haven't discovered yet with the iterator (is the order in which it processes it twice consistent?). title: Trying to understand the mapping of connector coordinates
body:
Hello,

This is my first time posting here, so excuse me if this is irrelevant. 

For the past couple of months, I have been working on creating a class hierarchy of a pipe system based of an IFC extracted from Revit. Picture seen below.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20814326/107385939-aa330680-6af3-11eb-8f07-f6f66e2cede0.png)

I've specifically created a class, for connection information and following coordinates class:

``` python
class Connector:
    def __init__(self, connector_tag, coordinates):
        self.connector_tag = connector_tag
        self.coordinates = coordinates>
```

``` python 
class Coordinates:
    def __init__(self, x, y, z):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.z = z
```

In the connector class, I want to extract the coordinates of the "IfcRelConnectsPorts", as the end of that pipe segment. And this is somewhat successful. 

I use this mapper to map the connections

``` python 
def connection_mapper(ifc_file):>
    component_connections_lookup = {}
    connectors_by_port = ifc_file.by_type("IfcRelConnectsPorts")

    for connector in connectors_by_port:
        init_in = {"inport": [], "outport": []}
        init_out = {"inport": [], "outport": []}
        
        outport_tag = connector.RelatedPort.Name
        inport_tag = connector.RelatingPort.Name

        outport_only_tag = outport_tag.split("_")[1]
        inport_only_tag = inport_tag.split("_")[1]

        if outport_only_tag not in component_connections_lookup:
            component_connections_lookup[outport_only_tag] = init_out

        if inport_only_tag not in component_connections_lookup:
            component_connections_lookup[inport_only_tag] = init_in
        
        coordinates = get_coordinates(connector)

        c_in = mapper_classes.Connector(outport_only_tag, coordinates)
        c_out = mapper_classes.Connector(inport_only_tag, coordinates)

        add_if_not_in_list(component_connections_lookup[inport_only_tag]["inport"], c_in)
        add_if_not_in_list(component_connections_lookup[outport_only_tag]["outport"], c_out)
```

I then use this path to retrieve the coordinates

``` python 
def get_coordinates(connector):

    coordinates = (connector.ObjectPlacement
                            .RelativePlacement
                            .Location
                            .Coordinates)

    x = coordinates[0]
    y = coordinates[1]
    z = coordinates[2]

    return mapper_classes.Coordinates(x, y, z)
```

The major problem here, is that sometimes I need to get the connection coordinates by the path:

``` python 
(connector.ObjectPlacement

```

and sometimes I need to use the path:
``` python 
(connector.ObjectPlacement
                   .PlacementRelTo
                   .RelativePlacement
                   .Location
                   .Coordinates)
```

and I can't figure out what the difference is. 

So I guess my question is: What is the behavior of this ObjectPlacement option, in relation to `IfcRelConnectsPorts`. 

I know this question might be a bit weird and unrelated, but I'm at a loss with the IFC documentation to figure out how this works. 

Best Regards
Mikki Seidenschnur

title: Bug report: fail at parsing IFC4x1 standard files
body:
current ifcopenshell v0.6.0 fails at parsing example IFC files provided with the IFC4X1 standard (for example https://standards.buildingsmart.org/IFC/RELEASE/IFC4_1/FINAL/HTML/annex/annex-e/wall-elemented-case.ifc). I ran the tests using python and the ```ifcopenshell.open``` function.

In these Part 21 files, the file schema is defined as:
```FILE_SCHEMA('IFC4x1')```
with a lowercase 'x' whereas ifcopenshell expects an uppercase 'X' (just changing the 'x' to 'X' makes it succeed).

A fix should target the following points:
* accept both lowercase/uppercase schema names (even ```iFc4x1``` should pass),
* raise an explicit exception if ever the schema name is not supported.

It is currently built with most options (but not the Collada support), against opencascade-7.4.0 (the one from the conda-forge channel), for python 3.7 and 3.8 Windows/Linux/OSX. pythonocc-core 7.4.1 (conda-forge) is set as a dependency and is installed as well.

Conda recipe: https://github.com/tpaviot/IfcOpenShell/blob/azure-ci/conda/

MS Azure pipeline: https://dev.azure.com/tpaviot/ifcopenshell/_build?definitionId=7

Anaconda channel: https://anaconda.org/tpaviot/ifcopenshell

The workflow I set up is the following:
myIfcOpenShell github fork commit -> MS Azure compilation farm Lin/OSX/Win -> Anaconda.org repository.

This is then quite straightforward to stay up-to-date with IfcOpenShell v0.6.0 branch. So far, there are *many* commits on my fork, I wait for the packages to be tested before pushing a pull request to contribute a clean conda recipe. There are also some required changes to the CMake file.

What I expect from the community is to:

title: Automated Blenderbim releases using github actions ci
body:
A suggestion for a Github actions workflow to automatically produce a new blenderbim addon release upon push to repo.

It will trigger the build process only when it detects a change in the `src/ifcblenderexport/blenderbim/*` subfolder or in the .yml file describing the workflow itself `.github/workflows/ci-blenderbim-matrix.yml`.

I have tested this on my local repo and created a test release [here](https://github.com/Krande/IfcOpenShell/releases/tag/blenderbim-210304)

title: Is there a strategy for recursive element remove efficiently?
body:
This question is basically a combination of #1228 and #944. In short, I want to remove an object from an IFC file. That object has a representation which needs to be removed. That's in theory OK, since from the feedback from #1228 I have code which does just that. However, related to #944, this object's representation is a faceted brep which has well over 100,000 vertices. So, uh, I press the button in Blender, and after 10 minutes my computer runs out of memory and swap so I don't know how long it'll take to finish :)

Thoughts? There needs to be a practical way for users to achieve this usecase of "let's delete an object", and more often than not the huge polycount object is the one you want to delete ;) Perhaps if it is known that a remove_deep is being performed, we can tell remove() to bypass a bunch of checks and "just do it"?

title: Decouple data and usecases from BlenderBIM Add-on
body:
As the BlenderBIM Add-on now does native IFC authoring, a portion of its code is 100% agnostic of Blender. I believe there is value in:

 1. separating the agnostic code into its own module
 2. introducing unit tests to make sure the code does what it does
 3. using that code to then generate IFCs which can then form unit tests for whatever else we think is useful instead of having huge test model repos
 4. polishing a super duper user friendly api for users over time to manipulate and generate ifcs at a higher abstracted level (that also considers schema differences out of the box) than the current offerings (e.g. pure ifcopenshell, and ifcopenshell utils) - this means refining how these usecases are called and even writing (gasp) documentation!
 5. Maybe we can even generate some visual nodes for this. Neat.
 6. Some higher level functions are useful in other utilities (e.g. currently ifccsv does its own pset and attribute editing - but with this higher level API it could do it better by considering ownership histories.)

The current system architecture is formed by dividing up the IFC schema into "modules" that delineate logical aspects of an IFC model that you might modify. For example, there is a module that manipulates the psets concept, and this is totally separate from a module that manipulates the classification references concepts.

Each module treats IFC as the source of truth. Two things are provided. There is a "Data" class for each module, which offers an abstraction to load useful information related to that module. It reads data from the IFC, and returns simple Python dictionaries and regular Python data types. The user can then use this as a cache of data, or a way to bulk load useful data without needing much knowledge of the IFC spec.

Each module also provides zero or more usecases. A usecase is a particular scenario where you might want to modify / write data to the IFC. It is higher level as it will take into account things like type conversions, maintaining ownership histories, purging trees as necessary, etc.

Here's a diagram of how the Blender-agnostic "Data" reading and "Usecase" writing concepts (purple) currently interacts with the BlenderBIM Add-on code (in orange)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/88302/111946724-29bee700-8b30-11eb-932f-8f2365a052f7.png)

Purple lines are data that use IfcOpenShell objects. Dark grey lines are data that are plain old Python Objects (POPOs) that aren't magical at all. Orange lines are data that uses Blender-specific data structures. Note how there is no coupling between Data (reading) and Usecase (writing).

Here is an example [usecase for editing georeferencing](https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/ifcblenderexport/blenderbim/bim/module/georeference/edit_georeferencing.py) and a [data class for georeferencing](https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/ifcblenderexport/blenderbim/bim/module/georeference/data.py).

The code is already written, but I want to propose splitting the BlenderBIM Add-on code from this core code, as currently the files are in the same place. Also the imports currently all have "blenderbim" in the namespace which isn't quite semantically correct :) This makes it difficult for a newcomer to simply include this library when they don't care about Blender.

So, this issue is to find out:

1. Is there anyone who thinks this shouldn't be done?
2. Any preferences on how this is bundled? Should it be part of the ifcopenshell python module, or should it be another module that is like an "api" to IfcOpenShell? Maybe `import ifcopenapi`? :) (literally thought of that as I'm typing this, no ideas yet)
3. Does this sound like an initiative that have some direct impact to something you're working on? Perhaps with the unit tests?

I was inspired to write this since @fbpyr seems to already be doing a lot of magical IFC generation and is using these usecases (currently through Blender operators, but effectively he is using these usecases).

Refactoring this is currently a low priority though, as nobody is jumping up and down for this just yet :) And the code kinda just needs moving and search/replace for imports.

title: BlenderBIM - allow to run without OCC
body:
This is a bit of a selfish PR... BlenderBIM currently doesn't run without PythonOCC. However, PythonOCC is a rather delicate package that needs some manual tweaks everytime a new version of OCCT is released. The current available version of PythonOCC relies on OCCT 7.5.0, but the version  currently in Debian unstable & testing is 7.5.1. PythonOCC doesn't compile with it.

It seems to me PythonOCC is used only for two operations: boolena-cutting an IFC file and writing to SVG. BlenderBIM could therefore be able to run without it, simply disabling these two functions?

This PR just disables the OCC imports at BlenderBIM launch. There is probably further changes needed in the UI too, so the correspinding tools get disabled to the user. So I'm leaving this PR in Draft mode for now for @Moult to orient me please ;)

title: Persons and Organisations account for IFC4 Schema
Importing Tessellation meshes is slow and generates additional geometry
body:
Attached are two versions of the same IFC mesh, this mesh has:

- 1948 unique vertices
- 2251 faces, consisting of:
  - 1977 quad faces
  - 274 triangles

A simple conversion to triangles would return 1977*2 + 274 = 4228 triangles

[_test_tessellation.ifc.gz](https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/files/6269744/_test_tessellation.ifc.gz) is a Tessellation constructed using IfcCartesionPointList3D, IfcIndexedPolygonalFace and IfcPolygonalFaceSet. IfcConvert takes 6.5 seconds to process this into a DAE file with 4240 triangles, there are more triangles than expected and additionally the resulting mesh is non-manifold in blender.

[_test_brep.ifc.gz](https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/files/6269743/_test_brep.ifc.gz) is a Brep constructed using IfcCartesianPoint, IfcFace and IfcClosedShell. It is a much larger file because this format is very inefficient. IfcConvert takes 3 seconds to process this into a DAE file with 4228 triangles, this is the expected result.

In principle, the Tessellation should be simpler to process since there is no need to identify and merge duplicate points, but the result is slower and less accurate.

title: blenderbim decoupling blender logick from ifcopenshell one
body:
At this time, it is nearly impossible to use blenderbim operators from outside as there are mix of blender's and pure ifc operations.

Some samples 
- bim.assign_class Operator also may create collections and move related objects to collections, rename objects and add some random magick making assuptions that objects are dumb ones by default - especially at project creation.
- bim.add_opening  create a boolean modifiers, however at this time geometry nodes boolean is way more effective to handle many holes, and other logick may also alredy handle the boolean part. 

Renaming objects on the fly will trigger "rename" handler, still not certain it is an isse at this point.

The "at class assignment" concept to keep virtual file in synch with scene approach make sense in blenderbim context, but it also require to "pollute" external code with blenderbim one and may not always be suitable / desirable from outside point of view. It also make pretty hard to assign / remove things on the fly at export time in order to provide a "for dumb" single button working exporter.

Proposed solution
At least keep operator's logick outside the operator itself as importable functions, and keep blender's operations apart from ifc ones, so it is possible to re-use core logick without actually re-implement when blender's operations are handled in a different way.

title: Brainstorming general solutions to the "undo" problem
body:
I have never designed an undo system before, so I just wanted to brainstorm if there were any "general" solutions which were able to save states prior to a change actioned by the IfcOpenShell Python API, and then optionally store it in an ordered list, and then restore that state if the user selects it.

Actions may be:

 1. Editing: element.Name = 'foo'
 2. Adding: ifc_file.create_entity("IfcFoo")
 3. Removal: ifc_file.remove(element)

Complex actions (remove_deep, copy_deep, etc) are basically just the three fundamental actions just repeated.

Naturally, the undo stack should store the final result of the element, such that if I do ifc_file.createIfcRootedFoo(ifcopenshell.guid.new(), ...) - the GlobalId does not change. Similarly, since STEP IDs are used to sync objects in the Blender client to the the IFC dataset, STEP IDs should be preserved.

Not an urgent issue to solve, but something I probably can't ignore forever :)

A naive suggestion would be that a flag can be set to start recording state changes. e.g. ifc_file.begin_transaction(). Then, the transaction consists of an ordered list. Each item in the list is either an "edit", an "add", or a "remove". The "edit" will store the element prior to the edit, the "add" will store the new element, and the remove will store the old element. Then, when all the operations are finished, state recording finishes e.g. undo = ifc_file.end_transaction(). This undo object can then call undo.restore() or something.

In theory this could be implemented in Python by wrapping all calls. This is however just my naive Wednesday morning idea of how undo systems work. I should probably do more research on it.

Thoughts?

title: first rough partial draft of alignment handling in python
body:
@civilx64 please have a look

I tried to work my way from the other end, from the alignment definitions connecting to your transition curve definitions. I didn't get very far. 

Some points for discussion:
- I used numpy instead of OCCT. numpy ships with Blender these days and I think we can get more eyes on the code if we settle on numpy, but for now it's not a major concern
- Since RC3 there is this separation between semantics and geometry. I tried to look at both, but I'm not entirely sure what to use. Also, with the nesting of the alignments you can either get the composite curve at the Alignment(Hor|Ver|Cant) or look one decomposition level deeper at IfcAlignmentSegments (which is I think is optional).
- Maybe I went a bit overboard with a functional approach of functors for the curves and higher order functions for the placements. I'm not sure if it really helps to hide everything behind a function interface (curve = f(u)) because you need more information perhaps on the outside to reasonable interpolate the segment.

title: blenderbim polygons not strictly coplanar
body:
Ifc expect polygons to be strictly coplanar, but in blender context you may very easly get non strictly planar polygons by eg editing any vertex location of a simple box.

In order to fix this issue we should add a set of 2 modifiers on the fly before evaluating representation and remove once done.

1 Triangulate
2 Decimate in 'DISSOLVE'  mode with angle limit under 1° and {'MATERIAL'} as delimitation.

title: BlenderBIM: TypeError related to `get_offset_point` when importing ifc file
body:
Hi,

in the recent dev builds of blenderbim (currently tested on blenderbim-210625 on windows 10 and Blender 2.93.1) I get an error related to the `guess_absolute_coordinate` method during import of IFC.

```
  File "C:\Users\Kristoffer\AppData\Roaming\Blender Foundation\Blender\2.93\scripts\addons\blenderbim\bim\import_ifc.py", line 499, in guess_absolute_coordinate
    props.blender_eastings = str(offset_point[0])
TypeError: 'float' object is not subscriptable
```

I suspect it is linked to the `get_offset_point` method returning what seems to be a single float,

https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/6e4e6a88a4f5b7fac2ff1f3d5164cc668f7e000e/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/import_ifc.py#L523

or here

https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/6e4e6a88a4f5b7fac2ff1f3d5164cc668f7e000e/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/import_ifc.py#L537


while the return variable `offset_point` used in `guess_absolute_coordinate` is treated like it is a list.

https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/6e4e6a88a4f5b7fac2ff1f3d5164cc668f7e000e/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/import_ifc.py#L497-L501

Manually changing the return value from `point[0]` to `point` solved my issue. I also noticed that my model is offset by default to (0,0,0) even though I haven't checked the "Import and Offset model". Is this a bug, feature or maybe some mistake in my IFC file? :)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9642232/123435064-6e459d00-d5cd-11eb-8f9d-22bf356a6587.png)

my proposed solution:

```python
def guess_absolute_coordinate(self):
        # Civil BIM applications like to work in absolute coordinates, where the ObjectPlacement is 0,0,0 but each
        # individual coordinate of the shape representation is in absolute values.
        offset_point = self.get_offset_point()
        if not offset_point or self.ifc_import_settings.should_offset_model is False:
            return
        props = bpy.context.scene.BIMGeoreferenceProperties
        props.blender_eastings = str(offset_point[0])
        props.blender_northings = str(offset_point[1])
        props.blender_orthogonal_height = str(offset_point[2])
        props.has_blender_offset = True
        props.blender_offset_type = "CARTESIAN_POINT"

def get_offset_point(self):
	offset_point = None
	elements_checked = 0
	# If more than these points aren't far away, the file probably isn't absolutely positioned
	element_checking_threshold = 100
	try:
		point_lists = self.file.by_type("IfcCartesianPointList3D")
	except:
		# IFC2X3 does not have IfcCartesianPointList3D
		point_lists = []
	for point_list in point_lists:
		elements_checked += 1
		if elements_checked > element_checking_threshold:
			return
		for i, point in enumerate(point_list.CoordList):
			if len(point) == 3 and self.is_point_far_away(point):
				return point

	for point in self.file.by_type("IfcCartesianPoint"):
		is_used_in_placement = False
		for inverse in self.file.get_inverse(point):
			if inverse.is_a("IfcAxis2Placement3D"):
				is_used_in_placement = True
				break
		if is_used_in_placement:
			continue
		elements_checked += 1
		if elements_checked > element_checking_threshold:
			return
		if len(point.Coordinates) == 3 and self.is_point_far_away(point):
			return point
```

I can make a PR on this if this is indeed a bug and my proposed solution is reasonable? :)

Best Regards
Kristoffer

title: Geometry serializers in python
body:
The geometry serializers (DAE, SVG, OBJ, gLTF, ...) have long been a IfcConvert only thing. In the 0.7 branch we will get access to them from Python. This will enable much more granular control over how and what is serialized. Especially in the case of SVG this will mean a great deal of efficiency when we can keep the parsed model in memory, convert to SVG, join the disconnected line segments to areas, and map the areas back to IFC all in one script.

For a sneak preview have a look here (Unfortunately on linux64 and windows builds for the moment)

https://github.com/IfcOpenBot/IfcOpenShell/commit/83049bf41a9feb2c2094a9ad7e9850e24745a651#commitcomment-53443187

TODO:

- [x] Next up is getting CGAL and svgfill (https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/svgfill) integrated.
- [x] Work out all the settings and serializer options

```
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom

ss = ifcopenshell.geom.settings(
    # this is required for serialization
    APPLY_DEFAULT_MATERIALS=True,
)

f = ifcopenshell.open(...)
sr = ifcopenshell.geom.serializers.obj("elem.obj", "elem.mtl", ss)

for elem in ifcopenshell.geom.iterate(ss, f):
    sr.write(elem)
    
sr.finalize()
```

or

```
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom

ss = ifcopenshell.geom.settings(
    # this is required for serialization
    APPLY_DEFAULT_MATERIALS=True,
    DISABLE_TRIANGULATION=True
)

f = ifcopenshell.open(...)

buffer = ifcopenshell.geom.serializers.buffer()
sr = ifcopenshell.geom.serializers.svg(buffer, ss)

sr.setFile(f)
sr.setSectionHeightsFromStoreys()

for elem in ifcopenshell.geom.iterate(ss, f):
    sr.write(elem)
    
sr.finalize()

print(buffer.get_value())
```

title: Tracking native architectural authoring
body:
To date, the majority of usecases for the BlenderBIM Add-on have been models authored in other software, and then augmented / analysed / etc in the BlenderBIM Add-on.

Obviously, the goal is that you can author directly in Blender. All the tools are almost already there, but aren't integrated. So in theory you could author directly, but it is an incredibly painful process and not practical. To make this real, this involves building more parametric tools, stress testing the parametric relationships (e.g. #1588), and creating a UX which allows for rapid, pain-free authoring.

The BIM Workspace Tool is at the heart of this. Here's a list in rough order of how I'm tackling it.

- [x] Walls
- [x] Slabs
- [x] Layer based things
- [x] Covering
- [x] Columns
- [x] Beams
- [x] Profile based things
- [x] Members
- [x] Openings
- [x] Door
- [x] Window
- [x] Furniture
- [x] Pile
- [ ] Stair

If something is marked as ready, it's ready for you to start stress testing and bug reporting and trying out as a native modeling tool. Please help and break it :)

title: BlenderBIM some data_dir / schema_dir workarounds
body:
Blenderbim creates a `process.log` file in `data_dir` when importing an IFC file, but it is not possible to change `data_dir` until a project already exists. My blenderbim is installed in `/usr/share/blender` so the default `data_dir` is not writable. 82dd395 detects a non-writable `data_dir` and writes the `process.log` file to a temp dir instead.

The GUI for `select_schema_dir()` and `select_data_dir()` selects files rather than directories. i.e. start blender, save the file `untitled.blend`, click Select Data Directory, close the dialog and `data_dir` is now set to `/home/bruno/untitled.blend` (which is a file not a directory). 703a66e strips the filename part from any path returned by the dialog.

title: Fix error if no ifc file set
body:
This aims to fix two problems with the Authoring sub panel in the Blenderbim N panel :
- If no ifc file was set, the panel logic would throw an error. Added a check in the panel poll method. This has the side effect to also hide the Architectural sub-panel which is a child of this panel. It may not be desired ?
- The code for populating the `relating_types` enum was accessing the `ifc_class` enum which would throw a warning and an error in case it was empty. We check for `getIfcTypes` items rather than `self.ifc_class` because accessing an empty dynamic enum throws a (very cryptic) message in console :

I've tried to make the BCF Project UI more foolproof.
Summary :
- Use `getBcfViewpoints` method to prevent the infamous empty dynamic enum throwing out cryptic error messages dozens of times per seconds.

- Use more descriptive variables to prevent batch-renaming mistakes
- Remove L.256 & 257 since the next step in the operator is to clear the collection

Illustration :
![BES_33](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/129627211-3f38a5e0-05d0-4a73-954b-6c2bf1228973.gif)

To go further :

- Is there really a use to storing all the displayed properties like `reference_link`, `related_topic`, `label`, etc on each and every topic ? They get overwritten and deleted on every collection update anyway, and only one of them is shown at any one time. It would make more sense to me to store them directly on the `BCFProperties` class like the Author and Project Name properties.
- It might be interesting to display a dynamic enum in place of the `related_topic` string field. This would prevent user from having to spellcheck the name, and allow topics with the same name to be chosen independently. Unless we don't want different topics with the same name ? In that case we should prevent that too ><

Food for thought :)

I think these lines are problematic:

https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/ifcpatch/ifcpatch/__init__.py#L35-L39

For example, if `args["arguments"] = ["foo"]` and the recipe signature is `def __init__(self, src, file, logger, args=None)` then it will call `def __init__(self, src, file, logger, "foo")` and so when the recipe asks for `self.args[0]` it will get `f` which breaks the recipe.

title: Improve drawing style save and load
body:
This one deserves a little bit of backstory :)

While looking for places where `bpy.context` was used instead of `context` when available, I stumbled upon the Drawing Style Save & Load mechanic (https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/module/drawing/operator.py). Initialy I didn't understand how it all worked so I didn't touch anything in the module by fear of horribly breaking everything.

After wetting my feet elsewhere in the codebase, I decided to dig a bit further and I managed to piece everything together (not that it was particularly difficult, but it was a bit daunting at first). The different drawing properties are serialized when the user chooses to save a new drawing style, and then un-serialized when an existing drawing type is chosen to be made current. 

However the current implementation leads to the use of magic strings and code duplication. I thought the `context` refactor warranted a little optimization exercise and that it was a good candidate for the `enum.Enum` class.

How it works :

The Raster Style properties are defined in one and only one place, which will be accessed by whichever other module needs to.
The enum members will describe the property they relate to, and their value is a string used in the serialization process to get or set the value.

```
class RasterStyleProperty(enum.Enum):
    WORLD_COLOR = "bpy.data.worlds[0].color"
    RENDER_ENGINE = "scene.render.engine"
    RENDER_TRANSPARENT = "scene.render.film_transparent"
    etc.
```

Importing the enum in related modules :    
    `from blenderbim.bim.module.drawing.prop import RasterStyleProperty`

Setting default values "by hand" :
```
        drawing_style.raster_style = json.dumps(
            {
                RasterStyleProperty.WORLD_COLOR.value: (1, 1, 1),
                RasterStyleProperty.RENDER_ENGINE.value: "BLENDER_WORKBENCH",
                RasterStyleProperty.RENDER_TRANSPARENT.value: False,
            etc.
```

The nice thing is we can loop over the Enum members to initialize the properties with current values, instead of manually setting them :
```
        space = self.get_view_3d(context)
        scene = context.scene
        style = {}
        for prop in DrawingStyleProp:
            value = eval(prop.value)
            if not isinstance(value, str):
                try:
                    value = tuple(value)
                except TypeError:
                    pass
            style[prop.value] = value
```

And the deserialization is also straightforward, since the dictionary keys are the actual path to the property :

```
        scene = context.scene
        space = self.get_view_3d(context)
        style = json.loads(self.drawing_style.raster_style)
        for path, value in style.items():
            if isinstance(value, str):
                exec(f"{path} = '{value}'")
            else:
                exec(f"{path} = {value}")
```

The scalability is quite manageable, since adding a new raster style property is as easy as adding a new enum member, and specifiying its path.

title: Optimising geometry iterator initialisation
body:
Typically with models coming from Tekla, I am finding that geometry iteration is extremely slow. I've dealt with hundreds of megabytes of IFCs from Revit, but Tekla seems to be able to pack a lot more into smaller files, though I'm not yet sure how. My computer will struggle to import an 80MB Tekla file, but will happily churn through a 300MB Revit file.

I'd like to investigate ways to optimise the iterator in this scenario, otherwise Tekla files become a bit unworkable.

I've only started code-diving, but this is my first time looking at this aspect, so I could be totally off the mark.

It seems as though the `iterator.initialize()` is already slow. It seems to spend a huge amount of time in [collect](https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomIteratorImplementation.h#L394) even before multiprocessing begins.

A few random sample files, I've also highlighted a count of by_type("IfcRepresentation") that has a non zero "OfProductRepresentation" or "RepresentationMap" in case it is useful:

Source | Stage | STEP Lines | IfcRepresentations | % | OfProductRepresentation | RepresentationMap
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
Revit | Consultant | 569435 | 7647 | 1.34 | 6903 | 744
Revit | Trade | 1911426 | 48038 | 2.51 | 45883 | 2155
Tekla | Steel | 1184489 | 308607 | 26.05 | 308603 | 4

The first one initialises in 1.2 seconds. The second in 165 seconds (not linear, it seems). The third I gave up waiting.

Note 99% of the IfcRepresentations in the Revit files are Body. However, Tekla exports a Body, Axis, and CoG for everything. Therefore, out of 308603, only 106568 are body.

Thoughts? I will continue to look, but thought I'd post what I had started looking at.

title: BlenderBim : Displaying empty dynamic enums consistency
body:
There is an occurence (the only one I think ?) where a property that has an empty dynamic enum displays in a specific fashion to let the user know about it.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/130194395-5c704ee0-15aa-4144-b063-9a41025e4a42.png)

This is done by using a dummy EnumProperty on the PropertyGroup
```
class BIMTypeObjectProperties(PropertyGroup):
    is_editing_type: BoolProperty(name="Is Editing Type", update=updateTypeDropdowns)
    relating_type_class: EnumProperty(items=getApplicableTypes, name="Relating Type Class")
    relating_type: EnumProperty(items=getRelatingTypes, name="Relating Type")
    # This is purely a UX thing
    blank_relating_type: EnumProperty(items=[("None", "No Types Found", "")], name="Relating Type")
```

Then the UI module decides which enum to display :

```
            if type_prop.getRelatingTypes(None, context):

                row.operator("bim.assign_type", icon="CHECKMARK", text="")

I wonder if it wouldn't be easier code-wise to display a simple label instead of using a dummy EnumProperty ? That way the property class definition doesn't have to suffer for a UI problem, and the information is conveyed nonetheless.

            row.prop(props, "relating_type_class", text="")

                row.operator("bim.assign_type", icon="CHECKMARK", text="")

title: Detect units from project libraries, and convert nested double aggregates
body:
See #1684

I opted to check project first, then only do the try catch for project library because there are two scenarios:

 1. A regular IfcProject which may have zero or more IfcProjectLibraries. In this case, the check for IfcProject passes and we're done.
 2. An IfcProjectLibrary, which there is only one allowed. In this case, the check for IfcProject fails, and we do the try/catch for IfcContext.

In addition, I found that length unit conversion didn't seem to work for cartesianpointlist3d, which I use in tessellations. I hope my fix makes sense.

There seem to be multiple potentially more concise ways of writing the same thing, like:

```c++
for (std::vector<double>& v2 : v) {  for (double& elem : v2) {  elem *= conversion_factor; } }
```

... or ...

```c++
for (auto&& v2 : v) {  for (auto&& elem : v2) {  elem *= conversion_factor;  }  }
```

... but I opted to follow the coding style already present, but please correct me if you have a preference or if there is a pro/con to each approach.

title: add (int() in IfcGeomShapes.cpp file
Display project units instead of hardcoded ones
body:
This is a draft in continuation of our discussion with @Moult on refactoring georeference unit attributes. I'd like to know if I'm headed in the right direction :)

Copying the conversation as a reference if you're okay with it :


> import_attributes will likely be used when the unit change is implemented, basically a callback will handle the map unit, and the code that handles map unit below it will disappear. There will also be changes in the UI to draw it nicely and purge the old code. Perhaps some old props will also disappear.
> 
> In short, the import_attributes brings IFC data into Blender. When the data type is complex (select, entity, list), it delegates to a callback. The IfcProjectedCRS has a MapUnit attribute with a data type of IfcNamedUnit. I highly recommend downloading the IFC4 ADD2 TC1 schema from https://technical.buildingsmart.org/standards/ifc/ifc-schema-specifications/ - or view the HTML online and check out Inheritance Listings -> All Entities and look for IfcProjectedCRS to figure this stuff out. Click on Attribute inheritance which is actually a link on the relevant doc page to show all attributes (yes, UX is a bit lacking).
> 
> Currently, the function has some hardcoded props for two dropdowns: 1) a unit type, and 2) the unit. Try it out in the UI now to get a feel. This is not very good since it always creates a new unit object. Instead, we want to allow the user to select from existing units in their project. So instead of two dropdowns, we just need one dropdown, with a dynamically generated list of all the units available. You can get all units from UnitData.units. Note it won't actually be all units, it'd be units which have a unit type of LENGTHUNIT. So the callback will set the data_type to enum, set enum_items to be this dynamically detected units (the value of the enum will be the IFC ID - the key in UnitData.units).
> 
> Let me know which bits make sense and which bits need elaboration. You can see an example of a similar (but actually more complex) callback here: https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/module/cost/operator.py#L653-L692 - that callback actually creates both a unit dropdown as well as a float, whereas we only need a unit. Also, we only need LENGTHUNIT whereas that cost example uses all sorts of units.
> 
> Making this change will break the edit function too (when you try to save your changes) but let's hack the UI first ;)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/130926376-8c3170f9-b471-47c1-8101-60da0119dbe0.png)

Now I think I've successfully converted the attribute to a regular one so it doesn't have to be singled out when passed around. I have to change https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/ifcopenshell/api/georeference/edit_georeferencing.py but it looks like a bunch of it is hardcoded and I guess I should just have to retrieve the actual unit id using DataUnit ?

title: BlenderBim Library : Issues in IfcProfileDef hierarchy
body:
I think there's a problem in the tree structure of IfcProfileDef types in the demo library :
https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/blenderbim/libraries/blenderbim-demo-library.ifc

![BSE_41](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/131330411-81417ae4-09f4-4d3e-bc76-7a9b9a151a73.gif)

IfcCircleProfileDef and IfcRectangleProfileDef are apparently referencing themselves, leading to possibly infinite recursion when traversing the tree. Also their children IfcCircleHollowProfileDef and IfcRectangleHollowProfileDef are also present at the same level as themselves.
I nosed around the Ifc file but I'm not fluent enough in ifc to solve the problem by tweaking values :)

title: BlenderBim WorkSchedule : Removing a parent task while editing a children doesn't disable task edition
body:
Here are two gifs of the problem :
![BSE_46](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/131670602-b77de638-4757-4d39-afc1-89c025abd45c.gif)
![BSE_47](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/131671808-60d1227c-eb0b-4728-9016-f276d5987e49.gif)

Removing a parent task from a Work Schedule deletes all its children. However if one of its children is being edited at the same time, the "editing state" is never disabled, leaving the UI List in a broken state since we need to access the now-deleted task to disable it.

I don't know how to fix this since I understand there can be complicated hierarchical relationships between tasks.
So either maybe :

- Prevent removing parent tasks while a children is being edited
- Force-disable the "editing state" when the currently-edited task has been removed
- Display the "Disable Editing" button at all times, not only when the currently edited task is selected

Depending on how easy it is to fetch hierarchical relationships between tasks using the API,

title: Filter by context id, not using curves or solids. See #1674.
body:
Work in progress. Needs discussion. Note: this PR is incomplete - do not merge, if you want to test it, you need to comment out https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/636d80093652db449168757dae6d1bb2dba788e6/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomIteratorImplementation.h#L325-L340 to stop the old behaviour.

Assuming you have it commented out, this implementation now allows:

 1. If no context IDs are set, all representations are iterated through, courtesy of https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/636d80093652db449168757dae6d1bb2dba788e6/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomIteratorImplementation.h#L365-L368
 2. If you set one or more context IDs that have representations, it only processes those, this allows you to filter out just things like axes, footprint, box (assuming we build box support), etc very easily. This solves #771.
 3. Because it only processes the context you want, in 99% of the cases you only want bodies, then fall back to other contexts, this results in significant speedups. This contributes to #1674.
 4. Because you specify exactly the context ID, it allows the user to have zero ambiguity (compared to include_curves/solids) about what is being processed and in what order. This solves #1290.

Sample code:

```python
s = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
s.set_context_ids([123,234])
```

Here's a screenshot of me pulling out just annotations (but not axis) from the test drawing file.

![2021-09-22-103158_562x316_scrot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/88302/134266995-a656e4d6-3d87-4f2f-8392-39f66e76fc48.png)

Questions:

 1. To expose `set_context_ids` I had to use `std::vector<int>`, then cast to set later. Is this OK?
 2. This implementation makes `INCLUDE_CURVES` and `EXCLUDE_SOLIDS_AND_SURFACES` obsolete. Is there any value in retaining them? One value I can think of is that it an easy way for users to say I want 2D and/or 3D. With the new approach, users need to be more specific ... 3D - what 3D? Body? 2D? What 2D? Axis? Footprint? Annotation? Target view? Scale? All? etc. This means the user (e.g. ifcopenshell-python users, and IfcConvert too) needs to do more work (select contexts) and filter on their end. Due to the uncertainty in this, I have not yet purged these options yet and not touched tools like IfcConvert.
 3. What should be the default behaviour if no representations are found? Right now:
    - Nothing specified -> Everything iterated (expected)
    - Contexts with representations specified -> Only those representations iterated (expected)
    - Contexts with no representation specified -> Everything iterated (? - I would expect nothing to iterate and initialisation to return false? If you agree, happy to make this change.)
 4. I know you asked "Something that also works with strings would be nice for the symmetry with IfcConvert." but I didn't fully understand. Is what I did OK?

title: Blenderbim tests assume startup file contains a cube
body:
Most tests that are related to blender objects assume there is a cube in the default startup file.
See https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.6.0/src/blenderbim/test/bim/module/void/test_operator.py#L100
I modified mine (File > Defaults > Save startup file) so that it contains no object at startup, so these tests fail when trying to select the cube.

A few ideas to fix this :
- Run a test blend file from within the test folder so we know for sure what it contains
- Create and use a brand new object for tests
- Test if the cube exists, and if not create it

I can contribute to make the changes if you feel like it's worth it.

Hi guys,

'v0.7.0-7155f7ce'

>>> p = f.createIfcPerson()
>>> r = f.createIfcActorRole()
>>> p.Roles = [r]
>>> f.remove(r)
>>> p.Roles
()
```

The cardinality of `IfcPerson.Roles` is `? L[1:?]`. Should the remove() call be intelligent enough to preserve the correctness of the cardinality? I.e. should it instead make p.Roles = None?

title: Drop obsolete pythons
Blenderbim : Handling incorrect parameters in operator execution
body:
Currently we have 2 ways (which are not mutually exclusive) of handling cases where operators are called with parameters which don't allow their correct execution.

I know that @Moult is working on a refactor of the ui-operator-file-data dependencies, but I wanted to write out some of my thoughts on the subject while the iron is hot :

1. 

If the operator doesn't have any optional parameter, we can use the [poll](https://docs.blender.org/api/current/bpy.types.Operator.html#bpy.types.Operator.poll) method to gray out the interface button, preventing the user from interacting with it. 
Example : https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/module/pset_template/operator.py#L62-L65
![BSE_48](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/135975537-94268687-0ab3-48ec-a495-b50bbfaec7d5.gif)
The implications I see are :
- It's clear to the user that this operator cannot be executed because it can't be clicked on, but they can't know why.
- Trying to call an operator in code while its poll method returns `False` will throw a `RuntimeError` specifying the `poll` method fails and that the context is incorrect. (a bit cryptic imo but I saw that custom poll fail messages can be set in 3.0 : https://developer.blender.org/rBebe04bd3cafaa1f88bd51eee5b3e7bef38ae69bc and https://developer.blender.org/D11001, although I don't know if the console error message will reflect that)
- It's hard to test these operators because testing edge cases throws an error, failing the test (eg in the case of RemovePsetTemplate operator, trying to remove a Pset Template when the file doesn't contain any fails the poll method, throwing error, failing the test)

So it's a somewhat good solution for UI based workflow (especially in 3.0 when we can set custom poll messages), but a tricky design for code-based workflow, as we can see in the test suites.

2.

The other solution is used when the operator has one or more optional parameters. The operator parameters are unknown at the `poll` evaluation time so it's not possible to use it in this case. So we return prematurely when something is wrong with the parameters : https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/module/void/operator.py#L26-L51 It's however possible to [display a message](https://docs.blender.org/api/current/bpy.types.Operator.html?highlight=report#bpy.types.Operator.report) in the UI when an edge case is reached : https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/cbc0b8d5d41be6ab32bc490d2952d63848293bf0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/module/void/operator.py#L46 However I found the user experience of these messages quite lacking, the info and warning ones are written in very small characters in the bottom of the screen and they disappear once the user clicks on the interface, and the error message is disruptive, opening a new window in the interface.

The implications are :
- The user can't be prevented from clicking on an operator which has incorrect parameters because the poll method can't be used. Theoretically the button can be disabled in the UI code, but that would imply that the UI takes more responsability than necessary, complicating the code (eg https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/module/void/ui.py#L42-L112).
- Since edge-cases fail more or less silently, testing the operators is straightforward

3. 

I guess the design question I'm asking is : Do we prevent users from clicking on buttons when the context is incorrect, or do we allow them to click but inform them when something went wrong ? Or something else altogether ? I understand some of these roadblocks will be solved once we decouple logic from ui and operators but I think the question remains as a design standpoint.

Cheers

title: BlenderBIM: Add UI Preset to Preferences
body:
So before I start making any real commits, I thought I´d first describe my idea:

- The user will be able to select a ui-preset from a predefined list which will determine which modules are visible in the user interface
- The user will be able to save their current configuration as a new preset in the list
- The user will be able to share their presets in the form of a .json file.

To do this I want to make the items in the ui_preset enum read from the .json file and subsequently write back changes if the user decides to update the list.


I´ve started defining the default presets [here](https://1drv.ms/x/s!AvVszTmf6whFhOIL1gH9lvKy9eqykg?e=yO9tGt), please feel free to edit directly.

body:

1- the add_work_plan file reference a method .get_person from the module api.owner.settings. the correct method is get_user **(Update I found this issue has been dealt with already)**
2- The IFC4D module and in particular the P6XML parser fails to parse calendars due to setting predefined_type = calendar type coming from P6. This is not correct as the predifined_type are defined enumerations in IFC4. Suggested solution is to remove the calendar type

title: [IfcConvert] Dae conversion error (Invalid cross-device) in docker
body:
We try to convert ifc file to dae with IfcConvert 0.6.0 inside a docker : 
`IfcConvert files/input.ifc files/output.dae`

Here is the structure (files folder is a volume) :
```
├── IfcConvert
├── files # it's a volume (-v docker parameter)
    └── input.ifc
```

But we got error : 
`Unable to write output file, see '.ifcopenshell.UBGGITYI.tmp' for the conversion result.`

We find a more explicit error message when we debug IfcConvert :
`Invalid cross-device linkfiles/ifc/output.dae`

`.tmp` file is created outside `files folder` (volume) and when IfcConvert try to rename it, it's failed !
https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/ifcconvert/IfcConvert.cpp#L1164
https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/ifcparse/IfcUtil.cpp#L334

Is it possible to create the `.tmp` file at the same location as `.ifc` file ?

We try to revert this fix https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/commit/ca85927a510ae0cb4a8f8f390186f3f8f2487278 and it's work 😮

title: IFC4D code refacotring
body:
There are two main changes in this PR
1. The code for creating the ifc entities for scheduling modules were repeating for different file formats. So, I refactored the common code into a separate class.
2. there was a missing attribute in the assign_process which implements IfcRelAssignToProcess. The missing attribute is QuantityInProcess. I have added this to the ifcopenshell.api. This is required to determine the amount of resources assigned to every task. The BlenderBIM interface will require update to account for the quantity of the assignment

title: BlenderBim-211027 Test Scale and Rotation
body:
Blender being an organic mesh modeling tool. it is very easy for users to forget to apply scale and rotation after creating or modifying an object. The exported ifc file will currently export the object as defined without applying scale and rotation, in most cases giving an undesired result. WISIWIG is great.. 

Maybe implement a check of Scale/Rotation before applying ifcClass. Maybe display a warning and exit Apply ifcClass routine.   

BTW it does not help to apply Scale/Rotation after an ifcClass has been set. 
However if You Apply Scale/Rotation after an ifcClass has been set, and make a Shift-D copy of same object, the first object will export without Scale/Rotation being applied, the copy will export as expected.

title: Failed to process shape
body:
Hi All,

I have been using ifcopenshell-python to parse IFC files and I received an exception error, "**Failed to process shape**" on several of the elements in a file. The following script shows two methods that I am aware of to extract elements from IFC. 
```
import ifcopenshell
import multiprocessing
from ifcopenshell.util.selector import Selector
from ifcopenshell import geom


def method_1(ifc_file, settings):
    """Method to seralize using the Iterator."""

    iterator = ifcopenshell.geom.iterator(
        settings, ifc_file, multiprocessing.cpu_count(),
        include=('IfcWall', 'IfcWallStandardCase'))

    walls = []
    if iterator.initialize():
        while iterator.next():
            shape = iterator.get()
            element = ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid)

            if element.is_a() == 'IfcWindow' or element.is_a() == 'IfcWallStandardCase':
                walls.append(element)

    print(f'Total number of extracted walls is {len(walls)}')


def method_2(ifc_file, settings):
    """Method to serealize using the Selector."""

    selector = Selector()
    elements = selector.parse(ifc_file, '.IfcWall | .IfcWallStandardCase')

    walls = []
    for element in elements:
        try:
            shape = geom.create_shape(settings, element)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'Element {element.GlobalId} was not extracted. {e}')
            continue
        else:
            walls.append(element)

    print(f'Total number of extracted walls is {len(walls)}')


def serialize(ifc_path, method):
    # settings
    settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
    settings.set(settings.USE_WORLD_COORDS, True)

    # file
    ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open(ifc_path)

def update_existing_property(self, prop):

primary_measure_type = self.get_primary_measure_type(prop.Name, new_value=value)

body:
Hello,

This topic is about BlenderBIM Add-on:
# Current behaviour
When you copy (`Shift D`) for example a wall type with a material layer set, the new wall type has the same material layer set assigned. This means that any change you make to material layer set on `wall type 2` also affect `wall type 1`.

I think that in common workflows you almost always want to modify thicknesses or material layers so material layer set of `wall type 2` should be independent of `wall type 1`.

title: The UI panel bike shed bug :)
body:
So I tried out the new panel + subpanel system today. Like the new direction! Some very minor meaningless comments:

 - Shorter titles. Sometimes Blender is on lower resolution screens and names get cut off. "IFC Collaboration and Data Exchange" could just be "IFC Collaboration" for example.
 - I'd prefer panels to disappear when not applicable such as before an IFC project exists. Otherwise it pollutes Vanilla Blender.
 - Would prefer the "IFC Project Setup" to panel to be open by default. It is the most important panel to be visible to newcomers and the first thing you look for.
 - Similarly would prefer the IFC Object attributes to be open by default as well as ordered first. On my machine "IFC Geometry and Spatial Structure" is ordered first which feels weird since the IFC Class is usually the first thing you look for.
 - IFC Systems not be under IFC utilities. It should be in its own top level panel for IFC Services (mech, elec, hyd, fire, comms)

Very low priority and feel free to disagree, you've been using the new layout longer than I have :)

title: Dynamic tooltips for attribute and property descriptions
body:
Here's a fun challenge if someone is up to it. It would be nice to have tooltips which annotate various things in IFC. There's two challenges to this: 1) getting the descriptions to use for tooltips, and 2) doing dynamic tooltips in Blender.

For the second, @Gorgious56 has done some sleuthing and this reregistration seems to be the way to go: https://community.osarch.org/discussion/comment/9204/#Comment_9204

For getting the tooltips, I wrote this little script a while back which scrapes the downloaded HTML docs from technical.buildingsmart.org. It's annoying we have to do this, but buildingSMART doesn't give these descriptions in any other parsable way.

https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/blenderbim/extract.py

I also produced https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/schema/entity_descriptions.json and https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/v0.7.0/src/blenderbim/blenderbim/bim/schema/enum_descriptions.json somehow from somewhere.

Property descriptions can be extracted from pset template definitions.

title: Improve section cutaway shader
body:
Following https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/issues/1997 and #1995

The Section Cutaway features are :

- Section shader must accept an input object, which will be used to make the geometry under its local Z axis transparent

- Backfaces must be drawn in another color defined in context.scene.BIMProperties.section_plane_colour

- Section shaders must stack

Summary of the PR :

- Optimize node network (removed ~8 nodes)

- Make node network "human readable" by tweaking the node positions
Before :
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/150695918-1fa2a81d-7f44-46f8-ae2f-5f786b8ae366.png)
After :
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/150695888-d621bf1e-c6df-4ae4-980a-70fc60389240.png)

- Dynamically update the backface color of the cutaway from the interface
![BES_56](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/150695980-bcc10b8f-4903-4722-aa19-ea1818241e63.gif)

- Do not forcefully delete objects that are not a section cutway object from the "Remove Temporary Section" button

- Rearrange nodes neatly when deleting section objects
![BES_57](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25156105/150696039-3f9d6c2a-4e86-4de2-a3c2-ab228384a1dc.gif)

- Add tooltips to both operators

- Rename operator classes to adhere to blender guidelines

Possible improvements :

A lot of the code relies on fetching nodes and objects by name, which will throw errors if they are modified. It is unfortunately one of the problems of the node system. I think it's fair to assume that if the user is bold enough to modify things in the shader editor, they should be able to un-break things afterwards :p

title: BlenderBIM: Dedicated Documentation Website
body:
Let's spitball some ideas for how best to go about this. 

So, @Moult has said he would like to emulate Blender's documentation. 
They use Sphinx
https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/
which has the nice benefit of autogenerating documentation based on docstrings in the code
https://betterprogramming.pub/auto-documenting-a-python-project-using-sphinx-8878f9ddc6e9

I do have some experience with setting up wikis and would consider myself an intermediate level python coder, so I can try and take some amount of ownership over this initiative. Definitely need to know some more details about how @Moult plans on hosting the documentation itself and any embedded media.

As far as documentation style goes, I'm not a huge fan of how much knowledge is now tied up in YouTube videos. If I were writing an article on how to use a particular function. I would plan on writing out descriptive steps paired with many tightly cropped screenshots and gifs or a more modern alternative (WebP?). It would be great to have regular links to the relevant IFC spec documentation for related features in BlenderBIM. Thoughts?

body:
Hi,

When I use IfcPatch to export IfcDoor or IfcWindow, it returns exit code -1073740791 (0xC0000409). However, exporting IfcWall works fine. Is this a bug or there is something wrong? Here is my code and the IfcOpnShell-python version I used is v7.0.0.

```
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.api
import ifcopenshell.util.selector


class Patcher:
    def __init__(self, file, guid, query: str = ".IfcDoor"):
        """Extract Elements

        Extract a subset of elements from an existing IFC data set and save it to a new IFC file.

        :param query: A query to select the subset of IFC elements.
        """
        self.file = file
        self.guid = guid
        self.query = query

    def patch(self):
        self.contained_ins = {}
        self.aggregates = {}
        self.new = ifcopenshell.file(schema=self.file.wrapped_data.schema)
        self.owner_history = None
        for owner_history in self.file.by_type("IfcOwnerHistory"):
            self.owner_history = self.new.add(owner_history)
            break
        selector = ifcopenshell.util.selector.Selector()
        for element in selector.parse(self.file, self.query):
            self.add_element(element)
        # for guid in self.guid:
        #     element = self.file.by_guid(guid)
        #     self.add_element(element)
        self.create_spatial_tree()
        self.file = self.new

    def add_element(self, element):
        new_element = ifcopenshell.api.run("project.append_asset", self.new, library=self.file, element=element)
        if not new_element:
            return
        for rel in element.ContainedInStructure:
            spatial_element = rel.RelatingStructure
            new_spatial_element = self.new.add(spatial_element)
            self.contained_ins.setdefault(spatial_element.GlobalId, set()).add(new_element)
            self.add_spatial_tree(spatial_element, new_spatial_element)
        for rel in element.Decomposes:
            ifcopenshell.api.run("project.append_asset", self.new, library=self.file, element=rel.RelatingObject)
            self.aggregates.setdefault(rel.RelatingObject.GlobalId, set()).add(new_element)

    def add_spatial_tree(self, spatial_element, new_spatial_element):
        for rel in spatial_element.Decomposes:
            new = self.new.add(rel.RelatingObject)
            self.aggregates.setdefault(rel.RelatingObject.GlobalId, set()).add(new_spatial_element)
            self.add_spatial_tree(rel.RelatingObject, new)

    def create_spatial_tree(self):
        for relating_structure, related_elements in self.contained_ins.items():
            self.new.createIfcRelContainedInSpatialStructure(
                ifcopenshell.guid.new(),
                self.owner_history,
                None,
                None,
                list(related_elements),
                self.new.by_guid(relating_structure),
            )
        for relating_object, related_objects in self.aggregates.items():
            self.new.createIfcRelAggregates(
                ifcopenshell.guid.new(),
                self.owner_history,
                None,
                None,
                self.new.by_guid(relating_object),
                list(related_objects),
            )


if __name__ == '__main__':
    fn = r"D:\code\bimsc\ifc_model\duplex.ifc"
    # fn = r"D:\code\bimsc\ifc_model\house5.ifc"
    # fn = r"D:\code\bimsc\ifc_model\cottage\cottage.ifc"
    f = ifcopenshell.open(fn)
    guid = ['1CZILmCaHETO8tf3SgGEWh']
    patcher = Patcher(f, guid)
    patcher.patch()
    new = patcher.file
    new_products = new.by_type('IfcProduct')
    new.write('tmp-wall.ifc')
```

v1.21.0

NumPy 1.21.0 Release Notes

The NumPy 1.21.0 release highlights are

  • continued SIMD work covering more functions and platforms,
  • initial work on the new dtype infrastructure and casting,
  • universal2 wheels for Python 3.8 and Python 3.9 on Mac,
  • improved documentation,
  • improved annotations,
  • new PCG64DXSM bitgenerator for random numbers.

In addition there are the usual large number of bug fixes and other improvements.

The Python versions supported for this release are 3.7-3.9. Official support for Python 3.10 will be added when it is released.

:warning: Warning: there are unresolved problems compiling NumPy 1.21.0 with gcc-11.1 .

  • Optimization level -O3 results in many wrong warnings when running the tests.
  • On some hardware NumPy will hang in an infinite loop.

New functions

Add PCG64DXSM BitGenerator

Uses of the PCG64 BitGenerator in a massively-parallel context have been shown to have statistical weaknesses that were not apparent at the first release in numpy 1.17. Most users will never observe this weakness and are safe to continue to use PCG64. We have introduced a new PCG64DXSM BitGenerator that will eventually become the new default BitGenerator implementation used by default_rng in future releases. PCG64DXSM solves the statistical weakness while preserving the performance and the features of PCG64.

See upgrading-pcg64 for more details.

(gh-18906)

body:
Bumps [numpy](https://github.com/numpy/numpy) from 1.21.0 to 1.22.0.
Release notes

Sourced from numpy's releases.

v1.22.0

NumPy 1.22.0 Release Notes

NumPy 1.22.0 is a big release featuring the work of 153 contributors spread over 609 pull requests. There have been many improvements, highlights are:

  • Annotations of the main namespace are essentially complete. Upstream is a moving target, so there will likely be further improvements, but the major work is done. This is probably the most user visible enhancement in this release.
  • A preliminary version of the proposed Array-API is provided. This is a step in creating a standard collection of functions that can be used across application such as CuPy and JAX.
  • NumPy now has a DLPack backend. DLPack provides a common interchange format for array (tensor) data.
  • New methods for quantile, percentile, and related functions. The new methods provide a complete set of the methods commonly found in the literature.
  • A new configurable allocator for use by downstream projects.

These are in addition to the ongoing work to provide SIMD support for commonly used functions, improvements to F2PY, and better documentation.

The Python versions supported in this release are 3.8-3.10, Python 3.7 has been dropped. Note that 32 bit wheels are only provided for Python 3.8 and 3.9 on Windows, all other wheels are 64 bits on account of Ubuntu, Fedora, and other Linux distributions dropping 32 bit support. All 64 bit wheels are also linked with 64 bit integer OpenBLAS, which should fix the occasional problems encountered by folks using truly huge arrays.

Expired deprecations

Deprecated numeric style dtype strings have been removed

Using the strings "Bytes0", "Datetime64", "Str0", "Uint32", and "Uint64" as a dtype will now raise a TypeError.

(gh-19539)

Expired deprecations for loads, ndfromtxt, and mafromtxt in npyio

numpy.loads was deprecated in v1.15, with the recommendation that users use pickle.loads instead. ndfromtxt and mafromtxt were both deprecated in v1.17 - users should use numpy.genfromtxt instead with the appropriate value for the usemask parameter.

title: BCF - proposal to manipulate DOM instead of file I/O per operation to improve performance
body:
I there a reason why the `BcfXml` class directly writes to/reads from disk instead of having an in-memory parser and writer?

In one of my tests I had to create many (~46k) topics - not something that we will (hopefully) encounter in production, but it still... - and I have very long running times (748seconds),  60% of it spent `open` ing files for writing the files.

I realized that the various methods of `BcfXml` are completely reliant on I/O operations, and I wonder why is it the case...

Wouldn't it be better if all the operations were made on the `minidom.Document` objects (or even better, using something like [`xsdata`](https://xsdata.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) to generate the dataclasses from the BCF XSD and using them), then dump the resulting XMLs into StringIO objects and feed them to the `ZipFile` object?

I will work on a I/O-less version the next week for my project; if I'll got it right, I'll be happy to provide a PR, if it's of any interest!
